notable_claims: The University of Wisconsin at Eau Claire was sued in federal court over racist email, with the judge ruling that content-based prohibitions on speech cannot survive constitutional screening.
Purdue University previously screened outgoing Netnews articles to ensure nothing was 'grossly wrong' before later stopping the practice.
Case Western administrators deleted a post containing source code to prevent users from learning how to disrupt the local network.
organizations: University of Wisconsin at Eau Claire
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a comprehensive list of censorship and disciplinary actions involving computer use at various universities in 1991. The items include the banning of newsgroups like rec.humor.funny and alt.sex, the deletion of source code for security reasons, and student punishments for 'obscenity' or 'rudeness'. It highlights early conflicts between university administrative policies and First Amendment rights regarding digital communication.
classification.title: Banned Computer Material 1991 (end of year update)

identity.subject: Banned Computer Material 1991 (end of year update)

notable_claims: Text-based newsgroups are unlikely to meet the legal definition of obscenity under Miller v. California.
State universities are bound by the 14th Amendment when formulating policies that may limit access to information.
classification.summary: Mike Godwin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) challenged Iowa State University's decision to restrict access to certain Usenet newsgroups. The university had excluded groups based on potential conflicts with child protection, pornography, and sexual harassment laws. Godwin argued that these restrictions likely violated First Amendment protections for textual material.
classification.title: news policy at iowa state

notable_claims: Requiring a signed form to access controversial newsgroups may violate the Library Bill of Rights.
University computer forums should be treated as limited public forums where viewpoint-based discrimination is forbidden.
The practice of 'labeling' or segregating materials by prejudicial systems is a tool of censorship.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie of the EFF critiques a new Usenet access policy at Iowa State University that required users to sign forms to access 'controversial' newsgroups. Kadie argues that treating computer networks as library resources makes such restrictions a violation of the Library Bill of Rights and First Amendment principles. He specifically challenges the university's use of 'Standard' lists to exclude material based on perceived offensiveness or potential legal conflicts.
classification.title: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

identity.subject: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

notable_claims: The new newsgroup censorship policy was not approved by the Comp Ctr Newsgroup committee.
The University Computation Advisory Committee did not approve the policy.
classification.summary: John Hascall urges the community to protest a new newsgroup censorship policy at Iowa State University. He claims that both the Computation Center Newsgroup committee and the University Computation Advisory Committee rejected the policy before its implementation.
classification.title: What to do about the new Newsgroup Censorship Policy at ISU

identity.subject: What to do about the new Newsgroup Censorship Policy at ISU

notable_claims: Adult-oriented newsgroups accounted for approximately 6.83% of total Usenet traffic in November 1991.
Readership statistics showed that while alt.sex was a top group, it did not constitute the majority of network usage.
classification.summary: Lars P. Fischer responds to a claim that Usenet is primarily used for pornography, citing an article in the German version of EMMA. Using traffic and readership statistics, Fischer argues that while adult content exists, it represents only a small fraction of total network volume and user activity.
classification.title: Re: The USENET pornographic network

notable_claims: Removing a newsgroup is equivalent to banning a magazine from an academic library.
Stanford University banned rec.humor.funny in 1989 but lifted the ban after a committee recommended following library policy.
The University of Waterloo lifted bans on rec.humor.funny and alt.sex in October 1991.
classification.summary: In response to a student's inquiry about Usenet censorship at Iowa State University, Carl Kadie provides resources from the EFF archive. He argues that university newsgroup selection should follow established library principles of intellectual freedom and refers to precedents at Stanford University and the University of Waterloo.
classification.title: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

identity.subject: Re: New news censorship policy at Iowa State University

notable_claims: Screening Netnews for offensive articles may increase a university's legal liability.
Courts have found institutions free from liability when control of publications remains with students rather than administrators.
The Cubby v. CompuServe decision suggests that distributors without editorial control are not liable for defamatory statements.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a query about university liability for offensive Netnews content by citing EFF resources and legal precedents. He argues that exercising editorial control or screening may actually increase a university's legal liability compared to a no-screening policy. The post references the Cubby v. CompuServe decision and the Law of the Student Press to support the separation of administration from student publication functions.
classification.title: Re: Inappropriate Use by 2714sviatkos

notable_claims: University computer use policies should not override contractual guarantees of freedom from institutional censorship.
Students should be free to express opinions publicly and privately as per the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a notice from Marquette University regarding the suspension of a student's computing privileges due to an 'inflammatory message'. Kadie argues that restricting access for offensive speech violates academic freedom and contractual guarantees against institutional censorship. He cites the Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students to support his position.
classification.title: Re: Inappropriate Use by 2714sviatkos

notable_claims: Iowa State University's policy prohibiting 'rude' material likely infringes on Constitutionally-protected rights.
Federal courts in UWM POST v. U. of Wisconsin and Doe v. U. of Michigan struck down campus speech codes as First Amendment violations.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie challenges Iowa State University's policy prohibiting 'rude' material on university computing facilities. He argues that such content-based restrictions violate First Amendment rights and academic freedom, citing legal precedents against campus speech codes.
classification.title: Re: BS!

notable_claims: Restricting system transparency in academic environments reduces productivity and cross-pollination of ideas.
Privacy is a necessity in corporate environments but contrary to the goals of universities.
classification.summary: Eric Lee Green argues against restricting the Unix 'ps' command, contending that transparency is essential in academic environments. He provides an example where using 'ps' allowed him to identify a user accidentally exhausting swap space with multiple instances of MIT C-Scheme. Green posits that restricting such information hinders productivity and contradicts the university mission of free information flow.
classification.title: Re: System Accounting: Fascist Tool?

notable_claims: Contents of academic computers are private unless the owner chooses to make them public
Privacy is a right regardless of whether an individual has something to hide
Faculty have a right to refine research on academic computers before publication
classification.summary: Dean Gottehrer argues against the notion that privacy is only for those with something to hide, comparing it to Fifth Amendment rights. He asserts that contents of academic computers should remain private unless explicitly made public by the creator. This includes research in progress and files belonging to students and staff.
classification.title: Positivism, privacy, and the flow of information

identity.subject: Re: Positivism, privacy, and the flow of information

notable_claims: MUD traffic accounted for 30% of total network usage during a weekend period.
Interactive response times on 56KB connections were insufficient for real-time MUD battles.
classification.summary: Brick Verser provides network traffic statistics from Kansas State University to analyze the impact of Multi-User Dungeon (MUD) gaming on campus bandwidth. The data shows that despite policies prohibiting MUD play during school hours, it remained a top application by volume. The author notes that while T1 connections handle this traffic easily, 56KB connections suffered from latency issues affecting gameplay.
classification.title: Network utilization by MUD players

identity.subject: Network utilization by MUD players (was Re: Gaming)
